title: {{NAME}} and the Egg in the Garden
moral: Kindness finds its way home, no matter how far it has to travel.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a curious young boy with short black hair and warm brown eyes, wearing a green dinosaur-print t-shirt, khaki shorts, and muddy yellow boots — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} was digging in the garden when his spade hit something hard.

He brushed away the soil. It was enormous — bigger than a football, speckled green and gold, warm to the touch.

"That's not a rock," {{NAME}} whispered.

Very carefully, he carried it inside and set it on a pile of towels in the laundry. He sat beside it all afternoon, just watching. Just before dinner, the egg cracked down the middle — and a tiny stegosaurus poked its wrinkled nose out and sneezed.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} named him Spike.

Spike had four sturdy legs, a row of bumpy orange plates down his back, and eyes the colour of pond water. He was about the size of a golden retriever and smelled like warm mud and grass.

Spike followed {{NAME}} everywhere — up the hallway, around the kitchen, into the backyard. He knocked over the recycling bin twice and ate three of {{NAME}}'s socks. But {{NAME}} didn't mind. He had never had a friend quite like Spike before.

pages.content:
That night, Spike pressed his nose against the bedroom window and made a soft, low sound — like a question.

{{NAME}} looked out. In the distance, past the park and the hill and the tall gum trees, there was a warm amber glow.

"You want to go home," said {{NAME}} quietly. It wasn't really a question.

He got his torch and his jacket. "Okay, Spike. I'll take you."

pages.content:
The glow led them to a hidden valley behind the hill — green and steaming, full of ferns taller than houses and the low rumble of dinosaurs settling for sleep.

A large stegosaurus — easily four times the size of Spike — lifted her enormous head and made a sound like a cello. Spike ran to her and pressed his little nose under her chin.

{{NAME}} stood very still and watched. His chest felt full of something warm and a little bit aching.

pages.content:
Spike's mother lowered her great head toward {{NAME}}. Very slowly, she pressed her warm forehead against his.

Then Spike nuzzled {{NAME}}'s hand one last time. {{NAME}} scratched gently between his plates, and Spike let out a contented rumble that {{NAME}} felt all the way in his boots.

Walking home under the stars, {{NAME}} held something tightly in his pocket — a single orange plate Spike had left behind, still warm.

He fell asleep with it on his bedside table, smiling.
